Yesterday we learned that a judge has allowed a lawsuit alleging that the facial recognition feature in Apple Photos violates the state's privacy law to proceed, in a case involving $32 billion.

Despite the two companies being on opposite ends of the privacy spectrum, this case has been lumped together with Meta's use of facial recognition, and the court, in allowing it to proceed, fundamentally does not understand how the feature works...

Prior allegations against Meta

To properly understand this situation, we need to start with a lawsuit that dates back to 2015.

Because facial recognition happens on Meta's servers, and Meta is able to identify those people, that company actually did break the law, and ultimately had to settle with the plaintiffs for $650 million.

Apple is now being sued under the same Illinois law — the Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) — which states that companies cannot collect biometric data without consent.

Apple's approach is completely different

There's a huge problem with this allegation: when Apple performs facial recognition in the Apple Photos app, it does not collect any biometric data at all. As Apple pointed out in a machine learning research paper in 2021, the recognition algorithm runs entirely on-device.

Moreover, the iPhone only recognizes that "the people in these photos look like the same person" — it has no idea who that person is. Only the iPhone user themselves can assign it a name.

Apple Photos' privacy policy reflects this as well.

This lawsuit has been bouncing around the court system for six years, and it shocks me that allegations that are so easily disproven — just a few minutes of fact-checking would do it — can proceed.

The courts and legislators should actively support Apple's privacy-protective approach, rather than lumping it in with the privacy-destroying practices of companies like Meta.

This is yet another example of the courts and legislators fundamentally not understanding the technology they are trying to regulate. The most obvious example, of course, is end-to-end encryption. Multiple countries have threatened or even attempted to ban it, despite not understanding how end-to-end encryption works at all.

Of course, I understand that judges and politicians cannot be experts in everything. But they could call in experts, and what I find baffling is that lawsuits and legislative attempts with such obvious fundamental errors can persist for years without anyone pointing out the problems.
